---
title: "Quiz: scale space, blobs and pyramids"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why is there no single "best" σ for analysing a micrograph?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How large are a nucleus, a granule and the texture inside the nucleus?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Different structures have different sizes: membrane texture is visible at σ ≈ 1, granules at a few pixels, the nucleus at σ ≈ 10 or more. A σ that suits one structure blurs away a smaller one or sees only the inside of a larger one. Scale space keeps all σ and lets each structure pick its own.
:::

---

**Q2.** You blur an image with σ = 3 and then blur the result with σ = 4. Which single blur gives the same image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Variances add.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A Gaussian of $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$. The squared widths (variances) add, as for sums of independent random variables.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why is the Gaussian preferred over a box kernel for building a scale space?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can a box blur do to a bright line in a dark band?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Gaussian blurring never creates new structure (in 1D: no new bumps, dips or zero crossings) as σ grows, and successive blurs chain into one Gaussian. A box blur can create new extrema: a bright line in a dark band can split into two bumps. Then a "structure" in scale space could be an artefact of the kernel.
:::

---

**Q4.** Without normalisation, the LoG response over all σ always peaks at the smallest σ for most blobs. Why, and what does multiplying by σ² fix?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does blurring do to the curvature of the brightness?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Blurring spreads and flattens everything, so second derivatives shrink roughly as $1/\sigma^2$: the raw response falls with σ and small σ always wins, so a large blob loses to a small one. Multiplying by σ² measures the curvature in units of σ (scale-invariant), and each blob's response then peaks at a σ matched to its size.
:::

---

**Q5.** A spot is detected at σ = 3 pixels. What is its radius? At 0.1 µm per pixel, what is its diameter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Radius ≈ √2·σ.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$r = \sqrt2 \cdot 3 = 4.24$ pixels; diameter $8.49$ pixels $= 0.85$ µm.
:::

---

**Q6.** An elongated blob (a short thick line) gives several small detections along it rather than one large one. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which dimension does the Mexican hat "fit"?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The LoG responds most strongly when its centre fits the blob in **all** directions. Across the line that happens at a σ set by the width; along the line there is nothing to fit, the response is almost constant, and noise picks several local maxima along it. The LoG measures the width of elongated objects, not their length.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is the difference of two Gaussian blurs a good replacement for the scale-normalised LoG?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What are the two blurs needed for anyway?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$G_{k\sigma} * I - G_\sigma * I \approx (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 L$: it is already normalised by σ², up to a constant. And the blurred images are computed anyway to build the scale space, so the DoG costs one subtraction per pixel.
:::

---

**Q8.** A Gaussian pyramid of a 2048 × 2048 image down to 1 × 1: how many pixels does it hold in total, roughly? Why must each level be blurred before downsampling?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \dots$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
About $\tfrac43 \cdot 2048^2 \approx 5.59$ million pixels (the image itself has 4.19 million). Without blurring, detail finer than the new pixel spacing would alias into false coarse patterns (moiré); the blur removes it first.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that $G_{\sigma_1} * G_{\sigma_2} = G_{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}}$ using the Fourier transform.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The Fourier transform of $G_\sigma$ is $e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}$; convolution becomes multiplication.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\widehat{G_{\sigma_1} * G_{\sigma_2}}(\omega) = e^{-\sigma_1^2\omega^2/2}\,e^{-\sigma_2^2\omega^2/2} = e^{-(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)\omega^2/2}$, the transform of a Gaussian with variance $\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$. The inverse transform is unique, so the convolution is that Gaussian.
:::
